title: Shapes around a plant
objective: Use the shapes of gaps around a potted plant to check and correct its organic silhouette.

warmup.instructions: Set a potted plant against a simple background and keep the view steady. Spend 2 minutes finding two clear spaces between or around its leaves and pot; trace each boundary in the air. Spend 3 minutes sketching each gap as its own small shape, before drawing leaves. Use the final 2 minutes to compare each space's width and angle with the plant. Total: 7 minutes.

explanation: The open spaces around and between the plant are shapes you can observe too. Each gap has an outline, angle, width, and position; comparing those spaces can help you place an irregular silhouette.

Begin with a few large gaps, then use their edges to place nearby leaves, stems, and the pot. Add small details only after the main plant shape reads clearly. Keep the gaps light enough that their boundaries stay easy to compare.

exercise.instructions:
1. Place a potted plant against a simple background and choose a view that shows the pot and a few separate leaves. Keep this viewpoint steady. (3 min)
2. Lightly mark the plant's overall top, bottom, left, and right limits so the full silhouette fits on the page. Do not draw individual leaves yet. (4 min)
3. Find three large gaps: one or two between leaves and one around the foliage or pot. Draw each empty shape by following its edges. Hatch inside the gaps lightly so they are easy to compare with the plant. (12 min)
4. Use the gap boundaries to place nearby leaves and stems, then add the pot. Check whether the angles and widths of those spaces still match the plant as you draw. (11 min)
5. Choose the one gap that looks least like the observed space. Adjust the leaf or pot edges around it, then add only a few defining details. (5 min)

reflection: Which gap shape differed most from the space you observed?
Which nearby leaf, stem, or pot edge did that gap help you place or correct?
extension: Repeat the gap-first study from another viewpoint, using the same plant and checking which surrounding shapes change.

teaching.whyItMatters: The spaces between leaves and around the pot are easier to compare than a cluster of separate details. Their shapes give you another way to check the plant's silhouette.
teaching.connections: Lesson 2 followed the shoe's outer boundary. Now notice the spaces sharing those boundaries with a plant; this revisits contour observation while adding a second way to check it.

deepDive: Positive form and negative space are two parts of the same observed arrangement. A leaf edge that turns inward also defines the edge of a gap; moving that line changes both shapes at once. The gap is not an undefined leftover. It has measurable features of its own: width, direction, length, and position among neighboring leaves or against the pot. Looking at the open shape can be easier than naming and drawing each leaf, especially when foliage overlaps or has irregular outlines. You can compare the gap with the corresponding space in your drawing and then adjust the shared edge. The plant and its openings must still fit together, so treat both as useful evidence rather than separate tasks. That relationship can be observed.

A gap-first study does not require drawing every empty space. Choose a few large, clear openings that can help locate nearby leaves and stems. Mark the plant's overall limits so the page has room for the full subject; then draw the selected spaces lightly and compare their angles and widths with life. Use each gap boundary to place the form beside it, and check whether the neighboring openings remain plausible as the plant takes shape. If one gap is noticeably different, adjust the leaf or pot edge that defines it. Keep small textures and leaf veins until the major spaces and silhouette read clearly. The same process works from another viewpoint, but the gaps will change with the view. These checks remain useful later.

commonMistakes.mistake: Drawing each leaf symbol separately without checking the spaces between them.
commonMistakes.lookFor: Gaps disappear, crowd together, or repeat as similar wedges even where the real plant has different openings. Compare one gap before moving its shared leaf edge.

visual.alt: Repeated leaf symbols crowd the first plant sketch and make openings vanish. A second sketch leaves distinct highlighted gaps between leaves, which can be compared with the real plant.
visual.caption: When gaps close or repeat, compare their shapes with the plant.

selfCheck: Can you point to three gaps in the plant and compare each with its drawn shape?
Did a gap help place or correct a nearby leaf, stem, or pot edge?
Do the main plant form and the open shapes around it still fit together?
